message.content:
The **earliest surviving reference to Jesus Christ in a non‑Christian historical source** comes from the Jewish historian **Flavius Josephus** in his *Antiquities of the Jews* (book 18, chapter 3, section 3).  Josephus wrote this work between 93 – 94 CE, about 30–40 years after Jesus’ death.  In the passage—often called the “Testimonium Flavianum”—Josephus describes Jesus as a “wise man” who performed “wonderful works,” was crucified under Pontius Pilate, and whose followers continued to believe in him after his death.

A few decades later, the Roman historian **Tacitus** (Annals 15.44, written c. 116 CE) also mentions Jesus, calling him “Christus” and noting that he was executed by Pilate during the reign of Tiberius.

These two references are the earliest **historical** attestations of Jesus outside the New Testament.  The earliest Christian text that mentions Jesus is the Gospel of Mark, which scholars date to around 65–70 CE.
